title: Sorting with comparators
description:
Employees are records:

```java
// Employee.java
record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary, int age) { }
```

Write the queries in `Staff.java` using `Comparator` builders (`comparing`, `thenComparing`, `reversed`):

```java
class Staff {
    static List<Employee> bySalary(List<Employee> staff)            // highest salary first, ties by name
    static List<Employee> byDeptThenAge(List<Employee> staff)       // department A-Z, then youngest first, then name
    static Map<String, Employee> oldestPerDept(List<Employee> staff) // TreeMap by department; ties: the earlier name
    static List<String> topEarners(List<Employee> staff, int n)     // names of the n best paid, ties by name
}
```

None of the methods may change the list they are given.

starter.Employee.java: record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary, int age) { }

solution.Employee.java: record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary, int age) { }

hints: `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary).reversed().thenComparing(Employee::name)` reads exactly like the rule: by salary, reversed, then by name.

For `oldestPerDept`, a comparator can also be called directly: `older.compare(a, b) > 0` means `a` comes after `b`, here "is older". For each employee, look up the department's current one with `get`, and `put` the new employee when there is none yet or the new one is older.
rules: Build the orderings with the Comparator helper methods.
